author: tom
title: Exported talent: the China-trained players in the world top 100
seo_title: Chinese-born players in table tennis's world top 100
description: How many Chinese-born players are in table tennis's world top 100? Eleven counted: 24 women and 11 men learned the game in China, and where they play now.
standfirst: Han Ying's defeat in Montpellier is a reminder of how many of the world's best women learned the game in China. Eleven counted them, and found the men's figure far smaller and the women's exports getting older.
body: Han Ying's week at [WTT Champions Montpellier](/events/wtt-champions-montpellier-2026.html) lasted four games. The German defender lost 11-8, 11-4, 8-11, 11-7 to Romania's Elizabeta Samara in the round of 32 on Tuesday evening, according to the German federation. At 43, Han belongs to a group of Chinese-born players who still make up a large part of the world top 100.

Han was born in Shenyang in 1983 and learned to chop there before leaving China at 19. Two more women in the Montpellier draw followed similar paths: France's Jia Nan Yuan, who plays Sabine Winter on Wednesday, and Australia's Yangzi Liu, who meets Lily Zhang on Thursday. With China's own six, nine of the 32 women in Montpellier learned the game in mainland China.

The pattern holds across the women's game. Eleven went through the ITTF [world rankings](/rankings.html) published on 26 October and checked the birthplace and early career of every player in the men's and women's top 100. In the women's list, 24 players were born in mainland China and took up the sport there: 13 who play for China and 11 who represent other associations. In the men's list the figure is 11, and only one of them plays for somebody other than China.

The 11 women abroad range from Macau's Zhu Yuling, ranked 11th, to the Netherlands' Li Jie at No. 100. Germany (Han Ying and Xiaona Shan) and Portugal (Fu Yu and Jieni Shao) have two each. France has Jia Nan Yuan, Australia Yangzi Liu, Canada Mo Zhang, Singapore Zeng Jian and Monaco Xiaoxin Yang. Zhang reached the final of last week's Americas Championships in Lima, losing [4-2 to Adriana Diaz](/news/calderano-diaz-americas-championships-2026.html). The only man is Slovakia's Wang Yang, born in Anhui in 1994, at No. 88.
Near the top the gap is wider. Nine of the women's top 20 learned the game in China: seven Chinese players plus Zhu and Han. Among the men there are four, all playing for China.

None of this is new, and the governing body once tried hard to slow it down. In February 2008, at a meeting in Guangzhou, the ITTF ruled that players over 21 who switched countries could no longer represent their new nation at the World Cup or World Championships, and that younger players would face waits of three to seven years depending on age. Adham Sharara, then ITTF president, said the aim was to "push each association to develop its own players", the [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/article/628166/hk-hit-hard-ban-table-tennis-players-who-switch-countries) reported. The same report counted mainland-born players in 19 of the 48 teams at that year's World Championships in Guangzhou. The Olympics, which the ITTF does not run, were unaffected. Under the rules as they stand, players who register with a new association at 21 or older wait nine years before they can play a world title event for it.

The reasons players leave have changed little. China produces more good players than its national team can use. "In China, there are a lot of good players and it is very difficult for everyone to get a chance to play for the national team," Han told DT Next in 2017, while playing in India's Ultimate Table Tennis league. She was a chopper in a system that, she has said, kept few places for defenders.

Zeng Jian made the same calculation as a teenager. Born in Hunan and trained at the Shichahai Sports School in Beijing, she played for Beijing in the Chinese Super League in 2013 before joining the Singapore association in late 2014. "If I'd stayed in China, I probably would have never had the chance to compete at the Olympics," she told [China Daily](https://epaper.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202408/09/WS66b54360a310587c4dcfa865.html) at the Paris Games.

The ages of the 11 fit the timing of the 2008 rule. Seven were born before 1990, and Fu Yu, Portugal's No. 83, was born in 1978. At least six of the 11 had left China before the ITTF tightened its rules, and Li Jie was already playing for the Netherlands at the 2008 Olympics. Of those who have moved since, Jieni Shao left for Portugal at 16, and Zeng and Yangzi Liu settled abroad as teenagers, young enough for the waiting periods to run out early in their careers. Liu, born in 2002, is the only one of the 11 born this century.

Zhu is the exception. A former world No. 1 with China, she left the national team in 2021 and, after a break, switched to Macau, which has its own association, in 2024. She has since won WTT titles in Cagliari, the United States and Doha.

The arrivals have given their adopted countries medals: Han was part of the German team that won Olympic silver in Rio in 2016, and Li won a world doubles bronze for the Netherlands in 2015. They have also caused resentment. "Through the easy access of the Chinese to the national teams, table tennis is being hollowed out from within," Jan Vlieg, a former Dutch national coach, told NOS in 2015 (translated from Dutch).

Eleven's count leaves out a second group that may matter more in future: players born outside China to Chinese families. Germany's Dang Qiu, the world No. 11, was born in Nürtingen to parents who trained in Jiangsu. Lily Zhang and Amy Wang of the United States and Spain's Maria Xiao were all born outside China too. Peter Hubner, a reporter for the German agency dpa, told China Daily in Paris that there had always been complaints from local fans about the use of Chinese immigrants. "But it will be easier for the second generation of Chinese players to be accepted," he said.

The open question is what happens when the 1980s generation stops. Fu Yu is 47, Han 43. If the women's exports keep shrinking, the women's list will start to look like the men's, which is roughly what Sharara asked for in 2008. Whether the second generation fills the gap is the next thing Eleven will be counting.

charts.title: Players in the world top 100 who learned the game in mainland China
charts.note: Eleven checked the birthplace and early career of every player in the ITTF top 100 of 26 October 2026 and counted those born in mainland China who took up the game there. Players from Hong Kong and Chinese Taipei, and players born abroad to Chinese parents, are not counted; Hong Kong's Su Tsz Tung is left out because sources disagree on where she was born.
